\chapter*{Pronunciation --- a reference, not a chapter}
\addcontentsline{toc}{chapter}{Pronunciation (reference)}
\markboth{Pronunciation}{Pronunciation}

A \textbf{reference}, not a chapter. Each lesson names the sounds its word needs; this is where to look them up. German spelling is far more phonetic than French — mostly you say what you see — so this page is short.

Ids (e.g. \texttt{ch-ach}) are cited in each lesson's frontmatter \texttt{sounds:} field.

\section*{Vowels}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
\setlength{\itemsep}{0.35em}
  \item \texttt{vowel-a-german} — \textbf{a} = a clean open \emph{ah} (\emph{Tag}, \emph{Nacht}).
  \item \texttt{vowel-o-german} — \textbf{o} = \emph{oh} (\emph{Morgen}).
  \item \texttt{vowel-u-german} — \textbf{u} = \emph{oo} as in \emph{food} (\emph{gut} = \emph{goot}).
  \item \textbf{Umlauts} shift the vowel forward: \textbf{ä} $\approx$ \emph{eh}, \textbf{ö} $\approx$ the vowel in \emph{fur}, \textbf{ü} = the front-rounded \emph{ee} (same as French \emph{u}). (Later.)
  \item Doubled vowels are long; a vowel before a doubled consonant is short.
\end{itemize}

\section*{Consonants that differ}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
\setlength{\itemsep}{0.35em}
  \item \texttt{ch-ach} — \textbf{ch} after \emph{a/o/u} = a guttural sound at the back of the throat (Scottish \emph{loch}): \emph{Nacht} = \emph{nahkht}, \emph{Buch} = \emph{bookh}. After \emph{e/i} it's softer (like a strong \emph{h} in \emph{hue}).
  \item \texttt{z-ts} — \textbf{z} = \emph{ts} (\emph{zehn} = \emph{tsayn}); \textbf{s} before a vowel = \emph{z} (\emph{sagen} = \emph{ZAH-gen}); \textbf{ß} = a sharp \emph{ss}.
  \item \texttt{h-pronounced} — \textbf{h} at the start of a word \textbf{is} pronounced (unlike Spanish/French): \emph{hallo}, \emph{Haus}. After a vowel it just lengthens it (\emph{gehen}).
  \item \texttt{d-t-final} — German \textbf{de-voices final consonants}: a final \emph{d} sounds like \emph{t}, final \emph{g} like \emph{k}, final \emph{b} like \emph{p}. \emph{Abend} = \emph{AH-bent}, \emph{Tag} = \emph{tahk}.
  \item \texttt{r-uvular-german} — \textbf{r} = a soft guttural at the back of the throat (like French), or lightly rolled in the south. Often barely voiced at the end of a word (\emph{Morgen} $\approx$ \emph{MOR-gn}).
  \item \textbf{w} = English \emph{v} (\emph{Wasser} = \emph{VAS-ser}); \textbf{v} = English \emph{f} (\emph{Vater} = \emph{FAH-ter}); \textbf{j} = English \emph{y} (\emph{ja} = \emph{yah}).
\end{itemize}

\section*{The two big habits}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
\setlength{\itemsep}{0.35em}
  \item \textbf{Every noun is Capitalized} — \emph{Tag}, \emph{Nacht}, \emph{Morgen} — not just names. A spelling rule unique to German among these languages.
  \item \textbf{Final devoicing} (above): what's written \emph{-d/-g/-b} is said \emph{-t/-k/-p}.
\end{itemize}

\section*{The High German Consonant Shift (a decoding tool, not pronunciation)}

Not about \emph{saying} words but \emph{recognizing} them: German pushed certain consonants forward, so English and German cousins differ predictably. Learn it and you can guess across the two languages:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
\setlength{\itemsep}{0.35em}
  \item English \textbf{d} $\to$ German \textbf{t}: goo\textbf{d} $\to$ gu\textbf{t}, \textbf{d}ay $\to$ \textbf{T}ag.
  \item English \textbf{t} $\to$ German \textbf{s / ss / z}: wa\textbf{t}er $\to$ Wa\textbf{ss}er, \textbf{t}hat $\to$ da\textbf{s}, \textbf{t}en $\to$ \textbf{z}ehn.
  \item English \textbf{p} $\to$ German \textbf{pf / f}: a\textbf{pp}le $\to$ A\textbf{pf}el, shi\textbf{p} $\to$ Schi\textbf{ff}.
  \item English \textbf{k} $\to$ German \textbf{ch}: ma\textbf{k}e $\to$ ma\textbf{ch}en, boo\textbf{k} $\to$ Bu\textbf{ch}.
\end{itemize}

(This is a \emph{different} shift from Grimm's Law, which is the older PIE$\to$Germanic change shared by both English and German — see the \emph{Nacht} lesson.)
